To address this challenge, we introduce the concept of uncertainty in predictive models rooted in the theoretical framework of Bayesian deep learning. At a high resolution of ~0.3", the ALMA detected four distinct plumes of molecular gas, possibly corresponding to gas filled cavities based on their proximity to X-ray shadows. This interconnection suggests a fundamental equivalence, which we can express as the notion that imperative algorithms essentially embody a form of proofs with cut operations. This equivalence serves as the foundation for an expanded framework, which we call "logical pseudocodes." Each statement in logical pseudocodes is analogous to a step in natural deduction, ensuring correctness and safety in accordance with the original specifications. This approach can be seen as a natural extension to the concept of a computability logic web, but now incorporating the capacity for forward reasoning. As a result, the traditional notion of a computability logic web can be viewed as a subset of logical pseudocodes, encompassing only those codes that represent proofs. 
The main outcomes of this study are the definitions of logical pseudocodes, the demonstration of their equivalence to cut-free proofs, and the development of an automatic conversion from algorithms to logical pseudocodes.

It is unclear whether incorporating semi-supervised learning is still beneficial when combined with a large-scale language model. This study aimed to resolve this uncertainty by comparing three data-to-text systems: one that solely utilizes a language model, and two systems enhanced with a data augmentation or pseudo-labeling semi-supervised learning method, respectively.

The results indicate that semi-supervised learning yields superior performance in diversity metrics. Notably, when the training set of a data-to-text system is extended using a pre-trained language model through pseudo-labeling, the output quality scores improve. Conversely, data augmentation results in comparable scores to the system without extended training. Overall, these findings suggest that semi-supervised learning can enhance output quality and diversity, even when augmented with a large-scale language model. Notably, pseudo-labeling proves to be an effective method for leveraging additional training data. While data augmentation has potential due to its ability to incorporate diverse sources of data, its effectiveness depends on the specific data-to-text application. Overall, semi-supervised learning can facilitate robust training for data-to-text generation, and its application can be informed by a basic comprehension of the theory and a limited number of label annotations. and their counterparts play a vital role in achieving goals and guiding optimization. However, these tools face practical and theoretical limitations when it comes to dealing with complex objectives that are difficult to combine or reduce to one another. Philosophers have discovered a number of impossibility theorems stemming from this challenge, indicating that there may be no effective way to define what it means for an outcome to be beneficial without disregarding fundamental human ethics. As this problem has significant implications for high-stakes domains such as AI decision-making, the current state of the field offers few viable solutions and little guidance on how to address these issues. This dissertation proposes a new direction by incorporating elements from nonclassical logic to develop more robust ethical objectives, ultimately enabling the creation of machines that can embody nuanced moral principles. A central theme of this research is the relationship between the expressive power of logical formulas and the feasibility of impossibility theorems. This investigation focuses on four key areas: 1) the application of modal logic to simplify impossibility theorems concerning social welfare objectives, revealing new paths to mediate seemingly intractable conflicts between individual satisfaction and the greater good. 2) the use of nested modal logic to define more refined outcomes and tailor-made ethical objectives, effectively handling complex state descriptions and the interaction between utilitarian and distributive justice. 3) the development of a modal language to express fair outcomes, linking this expression to the existence of mechanisms to mediate conflicts and achieve a more equitable distribution of utility.

A simulation study revealed that the family-wise error rate initially behaves in a concave manner, before asymptotically becoming convex as the correlation increases. The observed patterns suggest that when non-negative correlations are present, Bonferroni's and Benjamini-Hochberg procedures maintain control over the type I error rate at a lower threshold than desired, underscoring their conservative nature under correlated conditions and offering opportunities for improved statistical power through adjustments for correlation. The effects of positive correlation on statistical tests' power are also discussed in detail. Additionally, our research introduces a versatile method for efficiently calculating p-values that incorporate correlations, which can be applied to analyses of large datasets and those with specialized correlation structures. This research aims to alleviate the common practice of ignoring correlations within the p-value calculation, thereby providing a more accurate understanding of statistical tests' behavior and potentially releasing valuable statistical information that was previously wasted due to conservatism. The methods presented in this research will enable a more powerful and precise statistical analysis, empowering scientists to test a greater number of hypotheses with the same resources.

The underlying source coding problem is represented by a confusion graph, illustrating how source symbols can be distinguished from one another. The adversary's ability to successfully guess the source sequence is measured relative to its prior knowledge, with this measurement maximized over various source distributions. The course brings together insights from cognitive neuroscience and systems neuroscience to create intelligent systems by combining human and machine intelligence.  The course uses a tangible example - a digital assistant that learns and evolves through ongoing conversations with an experienced software engineer while beginning as an effective analytical and problem-solving tool.  Over time, these intelligent assistants develop essential thinking strategies and learn to rely on intuition through lessons learned from their expert counterparts.  As a result, these intelligent assistants become capable of working side-by-side as equal partners - serving as cognitive enhancements and digital prostheses that help their human partners make informed decisions and access powerful computing tools more efficiently.  The course addresses fundamental questions: How can we create intelligent systems that learn and evolve on their own?  How can we design these systems to protect their human partners' values and safety?  What types of supervisory systems are needed to ensure their well-being and fairness? For domains with irregular boundaries, using a grid without a set pattern to calculate the potential by splitting it into small areas becomes impractical due to high computational costs. In this paper, we propose an efficient and straightforward high-order method for calculating Newtonian potentials based on Green's identity, which simplifies the complex volume integration into boundary integrals. These boundary integrals can then be computed quickly using the Helsing-Ojala method. Our new method makes expensive computations of near field interactions on an unstructured grid comparable to the time it takes for far field interactions. An essential component of our method involves using a high-order approximation to represent a function over a grid cell, which traditionally poses an ill-conditioned problem due to solving a system of equations involving Vandermonde matrices. Notably, smooth functions and a backward-stable solver for linear systems allow this approximation to be accurate over a grid cell when done correctly. In this paper, we provide a precise proof of this concept. We demonstrate our algorithm's effectiveness through several numerical experiments. It is worth noting that the highest order of accuracy and efficiency is limited by the order of the solver used.
